content:
Not everyone without a job is counted as unemployed.

The unemployment rate’s denominator is the number of employed people plus the number of unemployed people—not everyone who currently has no job.

To be classified as unemployed, a person generally must not have been employed during the survey’s reference week, must have been available for work (with an exception for temporary illness), and must have actively looked for work during the four weeks ending with that week.

There’s an exception to the job-search requirement: someone on temporary layoff who expects to be recalled may qualify without actively searching.

But browsing job listings alone doesn’t count as actively looking. Availability, what happened during the reference week, and job-search activity during the four-week period all affect whether someone is counted as unemployed—and included in the rate’s denominator.
